questions.worked_solution:
The function ${t}^{2}{e}^{t}$ is continuous on $[0,x],$ where $x>0.$ So, FTC II applies, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{0}^{x}{t}^{2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={x}^{2}{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${g}^{′}(2),$ we substitute $x=2$ in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(2) & ={2}^{2}\cdot {e}^{2} \\  & =4{e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus by Interchanging the Limits of Integration
questions.worked_solution:
In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
h(x)={\int }_{x}^{1}(2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{1}^{x}(2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{x}^{1}(2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{1}^{x}(2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{1}^{x}(2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-(2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${h}^{′}(0),$ we substitute $x=0$ in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(0) & =-(2\cdot {0}^{3}+{0}^{2}-1) \\  & =-(0+0-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To compute ${g}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u={x}^{3}$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}({t}^{3}-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{0}^{u}({t}^{3}-2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand is continuous on $[0,u].$ Therefore, by FTC II, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{0}^{u}({t}^{3}-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({u}^{3}-2u) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})\cdot (({x}^{3})^{3}-2({x}^{3})) \\  & =3{x}^{2}\cdot ({x}^{9}-2{x}^{3}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}({x}^{9}-2{x}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=-{x}^{2}$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{-{x}^{2}}^{-4}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{-4}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{-4}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(-{\int }_{-4}^{u}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{-4}^{u}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{-4}^{u}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{u}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{x}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{u}) \\  & =-2x\cdot (-\frac{1}{-{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-2x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus With Two Variable Limits
questions.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-{x}^{3}}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-{x}^{3}}^{a}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{-{x}^{3}}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $-{x}^{3}$ and $x.$

The integrand ${t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying the FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{-{x}^{3}}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{-{x}^{3}}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t)+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(-3{x}^{2}){u}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{x}^{2}{(-{x}^{3})}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-{x}^{3})+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{x}^{14}\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{3}+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=-{x}^{3}.$

Finally, we can compute ${f}^{′}(1).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =3(1)^{14}\operatorname{cos}⁡{1}^{3}+{1}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡1 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡1+\operatorname{cos}⁡1 \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus With Two Variable Limits
questions.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).$

The integrand ${e}^{t}$ is continuous for all $t.$ Therefore, applying the FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{G}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-{e}^{x}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\cdot {e}^{u} \\  & =-{e}^{x}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)} \\  & =-{e}^{x}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).$

Finally, we can compute ${G}^{′}(0).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{G}^{′}(0) & =-{e}^{0}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)} \\  & =-1-0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus With Two Variable Limits
questions.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡(x).$

The integrand $(1+{t}^{2})^{2}$ is continuous for all $t.$ Therefore, applying the FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{G}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}(1+{t}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-(1+{x}^{2})^{2}+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot {(1+{u}^{2})}^{2} \\  & =-(1+{x}^{2})^{2}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x))\cdot {(1+{tan}^{2}⁡(x))}^{2} \\  & =-(1+{x}^{2})^{2}+{sec}^{2}⁡(x)\cdot {(1+{tan}^{2}⁡(x))}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x).$

Finally, we can compute ${G}^{′}(0).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{G}^{′}(0) & =-(1+{0}^{2})^{2}+{sec}^{2}⁡(0)\cdot {(1+{tan}^{2}⁡(0))}^{2} \\  & =-1+1\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand $\frac{1}{{t}^{4}+3}$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying the FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{1}{{t}^{4}+3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\sqrt{x}}\frac{1}{{t}^{4}+3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{1}{{t}^{4}+3}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\sqrt{x}}\frac{1}{{t}^{4}+3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+3}+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}\frac{1}{{t}^{4}+3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+3}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1}{{u}^{4}+3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+3}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}((\sqrt{x})^{4}+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}({x}^{2}+3)}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\sqrt{x}.$

Finally, we can compute ${f}^{′}(1).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}({1}^{2}+3)}-\frac{1}{{1}^{4}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus With Two Variable Limits
questions.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{a}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $x.$

The integrand $\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{du}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}(\frac{u}{2+{u}^{2}})+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}})+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2x+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x).$

Finally, we can compute ${F}^{′}(e).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(e) & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡e}{2e+e(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2e+e} \\  & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{3e}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle\dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \int_2^x \dfrac {t^3} {t-1}\,\textrm d t$ for $x>2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $\dfrac {t^3} {t-1}$ is continuous on $[2,x],$ where $x>2.$ So FTC II applies, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{2}^{x}\frac{{t}^{3}}{t-1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{x}^{3}}{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus by Interchanging the Limits of Integration
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
\displaystyle \int_x^0 \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t  = -  \int_0^x \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\eqalign{
 \displaystyle\dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \int_x^0  \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t 
	& \, \, = \, \, \dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \left(-\int_0^x \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t \right)\
	& \, \, = \, \, -\dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \left(\int_0^x \dfrac{t^3}{t^2 +1} \,\textrm d t \right)\
	&= \, \, -\dfrac{x^3}{x^2 +1}.}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute $f'(x),$  we first make the substitution $u=x^2$  and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{2}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{du}}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{2}^{u}\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The integrand is continuous for all $t,$ so by FTC II we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(u) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(u) \\  & =2x\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus With Two Variable Limits
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $x^2.$

The integrand $t^2 + 2t$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{{x}^{2}}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}({t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2x({u}^{2}+2u) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2x(({x}^{2})^{2}+2{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x+2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{3} \\  & =2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=x^2,$ as before.

Finally, we can compute $f'(1).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =2(1)^{5}+4(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}-2(1) \\  & =2+4-1-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
